title: 🥀 Google not feeling particularly lucky
body_text: The Odyssey is a cruise ship that promised high-paying passengers a years-long journey around the world, but has hit a bit of a financial snafu, with rising fuel costs forcing the ship to take drastic measures . These drastic measures include “forcing all the passengers off the ship they have been living on for ages, evicting them and dumping them off in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, a location that eagle-eyed readers may recognize is the epicenter of the global scam industry.” Nautical mishaps and a sub-par passenger experience thanks to poor planning on the part of management? Yeah, that sounds like “The Odyssey” alright. Stocks had a rough Thursday, thanks largely to the very subject of today’s Snacks… Alphabet took a shellacking this week after posting earnings on Wednesday evening that rattled investors. The parts of the business related to the AI trade were humming along rather nicely, with the Google Cloud business hitting $30 billion in revenue, beating expectations from the Street, with the company saying it plans to spend more money on AI next year. No, the issue for Google is that AI is actually hitting its moneymaker: search. Alphabet whiffed on earnings per share , which came in at $2.12, well under the Street’ $2.99 consensus. It also posted negative free cash flow for the first time since going public. Within five minutes of the opening bell on Thursday, $511 billion was wiped from Alphabet’s market cap. It clawed back a little bit over the course of the day, but that was the worst day for Alphabet shares ever with a 12.5% loss, beating the previous 11.6% one-day loss record notched in 2020. While Google is a lot of things — business services, AI lab, lots of weird funky bets like Waymo — the profit flywheel that keeps the whole machine moving is ads sold on search. This quarter search was responsible for $63 billion of the company’s $128 billion in revenue. Search growth slowed, and revenue was flat, as AI chatbots peel off Google’s share of the market for this kind of discovery – including Google’s own products, which appear to be cannibalizing its key business. On the earnings call, executives were pressed by JPMorgan’s Douglas Anmuth about the deceleration in growth. “It's worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode,” replied Google Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler. “To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here. Our ad experiments have shown promising results, and we're now scaling ads within both AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and more queries.” Google’s concession that it was indeed feeling the heat from a traffic drop because of AI was, in some media circles decimated by the “ Google Zero ” phenomenon, considered to be a bit rich . This is, if anything, a textbook case of the Innovator’s Dilemma . AI was going to inevitably affect the number of people searching things on Google, and therefore it behooved Google to get into AI with the expectation that eventually that new business would eventually make up what’s lost in the search business. For the rudimentary B-School case study, just look at what happened when Blockbuster declined to invest in a streaming service. For a specifically relevant and directly applicable contemporary example , take a look at the number of questions being asked on Stack Overflow now that every coder on the planet has access to an LLM trained on every tech forum post ever written: Google’s chart doesn’t look like this — congrats to Google — but its search business ain’t immune to the forces at play here. body_text: For the rare gaming enthusiast who’s somehow in two minds about whether to bother with undoubtedly the most hyped videogame of all time, GTA VI, a new offer from telecoms giant Virgin Media might just tip the scales. According to a new post on the TV and WiFi provider’s Irish website, Virgin will give one lucky winner €100 (~$111) an hour to play the game when it drops on November 19, handing over almost $900 for a full eight-hour shift as well as a free copy of the game. The gamer can clock up the eight hours non-consecutively, if they so wish, and will be expected to post their thoughts on social media after they’ve played, tagging Virgin Media. The contest is only open to Republic of Ireland residents, presumably making this the biggest event for Irish citizenship demand since Brexit . title: 😰 Google and Microsoft's AI stress test
body_text: One of the hardest parts of life behind bars is going years without your favorite comfort meal. I mean, who would want to go a day without eating Vegemite, the sticky, dark brown tar-like substance made out of leftover brewer’s yeast? Australians, who often enjoy it smeared in a thin layer over white bread, love it so much one man convicted of murder argued it ought to be a human right for him to enjoy some in prison. Unfortunately, the country’s Supreme Court disagreed, upholding one state’s ban of the product in prisons. One of the reasons it’s banned, prison officials argue, is because it could impair sniffer dogs trained to find drugs and alcohol. Alphabet , the parent company of search giant Google, and Microsoft will report earnings today as investors are increasingly seeking data over vibes to reassure them about the continued health of the AI boom. Both companies are expected to report enormous increases in AI-related spending, raising a familiar question: When will all this investment pay off? And here is what the Street is expecting from Microsoft. $46.5 billion in capital expenditures, up 140% from $19.3 billion during the same period last year. $90.6 billion in revenue, up 16.7% from $77.6 billion during the same period last year. $4.71 earnings per share, up 14% from $4.13 last year. And here is what the Street is expecting for Alphabet: $55.2 billion in capital expenditures, up 130% from $23.9 billion during the same period last year. $127.9 billion in revenue, up 25% from $102.3 billion during the same period last year. $3.03 earnings per share, up 5.6% from $2.87 last year. Meta reported results last week and was punished after reporting negative free cash flow and outlining plans to continue spending aggressively on AI. Increasingly, the worry for companies betting big on AI is that they are taking on debt to fund a product that has not quite proven to be lucrative. But not all AI spending is created equal. Meta, importantly, doesn’t have a cloud business (yet). Its AI investments are largely aimed at improving its existing products, particularly its massive advertising business, while developing new AI-powered services. Google and Microsoft, on the other hand, may be spending a ton on AI but they’re also collecting checks from other companies who are also spending a ton on AI. That’s because they, along with Amazon have compute to sell other AI giants. And those deals represent commitments from big AI players to spend figures that can run into the hundreds of billions going forward. A huge amount of power in the AI industry is in cloud giants like Alphabet and Microsoft. These same cloud companies are also investors in, customers of, and suppliers to major AI model developers. Google and Microsoft can justify their enormous spending plans perhaps more than others: They don't necessarily need to build the next killer AI app to make money. They can sell the computing power to whoever does.
